newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian military seen wavering as premiers feud.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian military seen wavering as premiers feud.

text.p: Cambodia's armed forces have vowed to remain neutral if fighting erupts between the rival premiers' security forces, but there are signs the army might split if serious conflict flares, political analysts said on Friday.

A dispute north of the capital Phnom Penh on Wednesday led to a clash between armed forces units loyal to the Co-premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who head a deadlocked coalition government.

But while military analysts said the clash, which left several soldiers wounded, was more the result of a business dispute than a political row, the incident was a worrying indicator of just how fast the army might fall apart.
"They're already split," one military attach told Reuters.
Military analysts say that while the upper echelons of the armed forces might strive to stay neutral in the event of a serious flare-up, there will be pressure to take sides.

"The two defence ministers want to be neutral. They're not war mongers, but if it happens, I guess they'll have to take sides," the military attach said. Two men share the post of minister of defence, one loyal to each prime minister.
A Cambodian political source familiar with security matters said he expected local-level commanders to rally to their political leaders if major conflict occurs.
"The Ministry of Defence and general staff will want to stay neutral, but the men in the field, the field commanders, they will fight," he said.

Relations between Ranariddh and Hun Sen, already strained, have grown increasingly fragile as the two men jockey for support ahead of general elections scheduled for next year. They formed their coalition in 1993 after U.N.-sponsored polls.
The Cambodian armed forces is an amalgamation of old battle field foes.

The former army of the old communist government, led by Hun Sen, was merged with their former enemies, including forces loyal to Prince Ranariddh and another guerrilla army allied to the royalists, under a peace plan following a 1991 treaty.

Military analysts say the current loyalties in the estimated 127,000-strong armed forces reflect the situation at the time of the merger, with roughly 70 percent of the troops likely to support Hun Sen and 30 percent seen siding with Ranariddh.

Complicating the picture is the incorporation into the army of some 18,000 former Khmer Rouge members, including soldiers, militiamen and policemen, whose loyalties are still hazy although some analysts predict a majority would rally to Ranariddh.
The Khmer Rouge guerrilla force, whose 1975-79 "killing fields" rule left more than one million Cambodians dead, began to unravel last August after thousands of rebels defected to the government.
For the time being, the most likely spark for conflict is confrontation between the two prime ministers' well-armed security units, both of which number more than 1,000 men, political analysts said.
"My main concern is the private armies created around the two prime ministers," said Cambodia scholar Raoul Jennar. "These are people who just obey their boss, the man who pays them".
Security men loyal to the two prime ministers clashed in Phnom Penh on June 17. Two of Ranariddh's men died in that battle.

If a clash between the security units does explode into full-scale conflict, military analysts said the outcome would be decided by infantry units. Tanks, artillery and air-power, most of which are controlled by Hun Sen, would play a minor role.

"The number of tanks is of no importance. Tanks would be important for controlling the airport and you can scare people with them, but there are so many anti-tank weapons around I wouldn't like to be in one," the defence attach said.
"If fighting starts, it will be fighting with light units. Artillery will mean nothing, the real power is infantry," he said.
Forces loyal to Hun Sen are concentrated in the east of the country and around the capital, while those loyal to Ranariddh are based in northern and northwestern Cambodia.

"In a worst-case scenario, the only solution for them (forces loyal to Ranariddh) would be to retreat and stand in their old zones. There would be a split in the country like the old days," said the attach, referring to the late 1980s and early 1990s when the royalists and their guerrilla allies controlled large areas of remote countryside.
